title: The Banger Sisters
full_review:
The disagreeable comedy "The Banger Sisters" (Fox Searchlight) sugarcoats promiscuity as it reunites two old girlfriends, both legendary rock 'n' roll groupies from the 1960s who have now reached middle age.

The directorial debut of Bob Dolman stars Goldie Hawn and Susan Sarandon as the title characters. They are not related but teamed up in the heyday of rock 'n' roll to literally charm the pants off of every music legend they could, hence the moniker "banger sisters."

Decades later, Suzette (Hawn) is a bartender on Sunset Strip at the Whiskey A Go Go bar, trying to live vicariously through the younger folk. But when she is fired, the financially down-and-out Suzette decides to travel to Phoenix to visit Vinnie (Sarandon) to borrow money. Vinnie is now Lavinia, an uptight socialite, wife and mother of two teen-age daughters who has created a prim and proper past for herself in an attempt to leave her real one behind.

The forced narrative is clunky and predictable from the start. The reunion of the "banger sisters" is a collision of two women's worlds: one who is living in the past, and the other who's hiding from it. Naturally, Suzette upsets Vinnie's carefully arranged family life and reminds her of her former fun self.

In one of the few emotionally honest scenes, Lavinia is hurt and a little offended that her daughters -- Hannah (Erika Christensen), who seems to be following in Mom's old footsteps, and Ginger (Eva Amurri) -- and her lawyer-husband Raymond (Robin Thomas) laugh heartily at the thought that Mom could ever have been rebellious, much less know who Jim Morrison was.

Reverting to her old ways, Lavinia snips her presentable bob hair into a funky short cut, borrows some tarty clothes from Suzette and the two go out for a night on the town. There's something to be said for confronting the past and accepting who you were and are. Yet instead of seeing the advantages of her current lifestyle (such as not having to beg for money and having a nice family), Lavinia admits she's lost her true self while attending to her family. But to highlight the positive aspects of her life would be to acknowledge Suzette's failures, which the narrative stubbornly refuses to concede.

The movie would have audiences believe that Lavinia must channel the vamp within her to truly be happy. It is a superficial story which, while admirable for presenting women in their 50s as sexy and attractive, nonetheless relies on the foolish premise that only through living it up is one truly liberated. Although Lavinia remains faithful to her husband, when the two women pull out mementos from the past (Polaroids of former lovers' private parts) and light up an old joint, the story becomes more than a little off-putting.

Geoffrey Rush plays the neurotic writer, Harry, who Suzette picks up on her way to Phoenix. She applies the same adage to Harry -- that having sex solves problems and helps one to be the best one can be. But the cartwheels the plot goes through to keep him in the picture only emphasize the film's lack of cohesion.

Both Hawn and Sarandon are competent actresses, but their talents cannot compensate for the distasteful story, which remains grounded in an immature philosophy.

Due to some sexual encounters and several sexual references, fleeting frontal nudity, a benign depiction of promiscuity, brief drug content and some rough language and profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. 2002
